oneLineAnswer: A daily anti-anxiety medicine for generalized anxiety disorder. It is not a sedative and takes weeks to work.
whatItIs: Buspirone is a prescription anti-anxiety medicine, also called an anxiolytic. US labeling states it is not chemically or pharmacologically related to benzodiazepines, barbiturates, or other sedative drugs. Its exact mechanism is unknown. Laboratory studies show it binds serotonin 5-HT1A receptors with high affinity and brain dopamine D2 receptors with moderate affinity. A receptor is a docking point on a cell where a chemical messenger attaches.
whatItDoes: US labeling says buspirone is indicated to manage anxiety disorders or give short-term relief of anxiety symptoms.
That approval rests on controlled trials of outpatients whose diagnosis was close to generalized anxiety disorder, or GAD.
GAD means worry that is hard to control and lasts for months.
The label notes that stress and tension of everyday life usually do not call for an anti-anxiety medicine.
NIMH says buspirone must be taken daily for 3 to 4 weeks before it becomes fully effective.
howPeopleUseIt: It comes as a tablet you swallow, sold in several strengths.
Labels describe taking it in two or three smaller amounts spread across the day.
The label tells patients to keep food consistent, so always with food or always without it.
In US law buspirone is not a controlled substance.
NIMH notes it is not used only when anxiety flares, unlike benzodiazepines.

commonSideEffects: In placebo-controlled trials, dizziness, nausea, headache, nervousness, lightheadedness, and excitement were reported more often than with placebo.
Drowsiness, trouble sleeping, dry mouth, fatigue, and blurred vision were also reported.
About 10 percent of 2,200 people in the early efficacy trials stopped treatment because of a side effect.
A feeling of restlessness appearing soon after treatment starts has been reported in a small share of people.
The label says buspirone is less sedating than other anxiolytics, but its effects on any one person are not predictable.
seriousSigns: A rare, potentially life-threatening condition called serotonin syndrome has been reported with buspirone, particularly alongside other serotonin-raising drugs.
Labeled signs include agitation, confusion, hallucinations, fast pulse, unstable blood pressure, sweating, fever, tremor, rigid muscles, twitching, clumsiness, and seizures.
Blood pressure has risen when buspirone was added for patients already taking an MAOI antidepressant.
The label says buspirone has no established antipsychotic activity, so it should not stand in for antipsychotic treatment.
The label directs patients to avoid driving or using dangerous machinery until they know how the medicine affects them.
whoShouldAvoid: The label says buspirone is contraindicated in people hypersensitive to it.
It is contraindicated together with MAOI antidepressants, and within 14 days of stopping one.
It is also contraindicated with the antibiotic linezolid or intravenous methylene blue.
The label says nursing women should avoid it if clinically possible, because human milk transfer is unknown.
The label advises gradual withdrawal of any prior sedative or hypnotic drug before buspirone is started.

interactions: MAOI antidepressants carry the strongest warning: using buspirone with them is contraindicated because of serotonin syndrome and elevated blood pressure risk.
Triptans, used for migraine, need careful observation during treatment start and dose changes.
Serotonin precursors such as tryptophan are not recommended alongside buspirone.
Buspirone is metabolized mainly by the liver enzyme CYP3A4, so other drugs that affect this enzyme can change buspirone levels.
Patient instructions say to avoid drinking large amounts of grapefruit juice during treatment.
Formal studies found buspirone did not increase alcohol-related impairment, but the label still calls it prudent to avoid the combination.
Antipsychotics and other drugs that block dopamine are also listed among medicines to watch.
pregnancyAndChildren: The label rates buspirone as pregnancy category B. Animal reproduction studies in rats and rabbits at high doses found no fetal damage or fertility loss. No adequate, well-controlled studies have been done in pregnant people, so the label says to use it during pregnancy only if clearly needed. Whether buspirone or its breakdown products pass into human milk is not known, though in rats they do appear in milk. In two 6-week placebo-controlled trials of 559 children aged 6 to 17 with GAD, buspirone did not differ significantly from placebo, and there are no long-term safety or effectiveness data in children.
whatWeDoNotKnow: How buspirone actually reduces anxiety is unknown; the label states this directly.
Effectiveness beyond about 3 to 4 weeks of use has not been demonstrated in controlled trials.
No body of evidence settles what the appropriate duration of treatment should be.
How much buspirone reaches human breast milk is unmeasured, and long-term effects in children are unstudied.
A registered trial is testing a long-acting buspirone tablet for vertigo with autonomic dysfunction, and no results are posted yet.

summary: This record covers what buspirone is, the anxiety uses its US label and NIMH describe, how it is taken daily, its common and serious side effects, key interactions, and the pregnancy, breastfeeding, and child evidence gaps.
